headline: Waymo pauses driverless taxi rides on U.S. freeways

sources.title: Waymo temporarily pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways (BBC News)
California bans Waymo self-driving cars from freeways (The Guardian)
Waymo pauses robotaxi rides on US freeways after California ban (CNA)

chunks.text: On November 17, 2026, the [[driverless]] taxi company Waymo said it had {{called off}} all rides on U.S. freeways, the big, fast highways with no traffic lights. Waymo said the [[pause]] was [[temporary]]. Waymo has the same owner as Google. It runs the country's largest group, or [[fleet]], of self-driving cars. The decision came after California officials {{stepped in}} and [[banned]] its driverless cars from every state freeway.

verbs.wrong: To paint a car a new color
verbs.why: Schools call off classes when a big storm comes. Coaches call off practice on very hot days. Waymo said it had called off all its freeway rides.

verbs.correct: To act to stop a problem
verbs.wrong: To leave a job in government
verbs.why: A teacher steps in when two students start to fight. The city steps in when a building becomes unsafe. California officials stepped in and banned Waymo's driverless cars from state freeways.

chunks.text: California's motor vehicle department called Waymo's freeway service an "[[imminent hazard]] to [[public safety]]," a danger that could soon hurt people. The ban {{kicked in}} on November 11. On November 5, three Waymo cars had {{ended up}} in a [[construction zone]] south of San Francisco. That is part of a road closed for [[repair work]], with workers and machines nearby. Waymo {{pointed out}} that nobody was hurt and no cars crashed. A video from November 6 appeared to show a Waymo car trying to {{get around}} [[highway patrol]] cars, state police cars that were slowing traffic [[on purpose]].

verbs.wrong: To be painted a bright color
verbs.why: The medicine kicks in after about 20 minutes. A new rule often kicks in on the first day of the year. California's ban on Waymo's driverless cars kicked in on November 11.

verbs.correct: To arrive somewhere without planning it
verbs.wrong: To be sold cheaply to a new owner
verbs.why: Tourists often end up on the wrong train. Lost hikers sometimes end up far from their camp. Three Waymo cars ended up in a construction zone south of San Francisco.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.wrong: To pay a fine to the state
verbs.why: Doctors point out that sleep is important for good health. My sister always points out that the store closes early on Sundays. Waymo pointed out that nobody was hurt in the construction zone.

verbs.correct: To avoid something blocking your way
verbs.wrong: To play loud music on a car radio
verbs.why: Drivers get around a fallen tree by using the other lane. Bike riders get around parked cars every day. A video appeared to show a Waymo car trying to get around highway patrol cars.

chunks.text: Waymo {{rolled out}} freeway rides in 2025. By November 2026, it operated in 15 U.S. cities, but only a few had freeway trips, including San Francisco and Los Angeles. Waymo said it stopped those trips outside California so it could {{look into}} how its cars were [[performing]]. Its taxis continued to use regular city streets. Waymo's website says its cars have 95 percent fewer crashes with [[serious injuries]] than human drivers.

verbs.correct: To offer a new service to the public
verbs.wrong: To draw a picture of a new service
verbs.why: Phone companies roll out new plans every year. Banks roll out new apps for their customers. Waymo rolled out freeway rides in 2025.

verbs.correct: To study something to learn more
verbs.wrong: To buy new parts for a car
verbs.why: The police look into every report of a stolen car. My manager looks into each complaint from a customer. Waymo said it stopped freeway trips so it could look into how its cars were performing.

chunks.text: California said the ban would stay until Waymo showed it had made [[effective]] changes. The state said similar [[incidents]] happened on May 18, 2026. Waymo said it was working with officials to {{bring back}} freeway rides. The pause {{set back}} a company trying to [[expand]] quickly. It came as [[rivals]] such as Tesla and Amazon were trying to {{catch up}} with it.

verbs.wrong: To draw something on a road map
verbs.why: The cafe brings back its pumpkin soup every fall. Our gym brings back evening classes in January. Waymo said it was working with state officials to bring back freeway rides.

verbs.wrong: To move a company to a new city
verbs.why: Bad weather sets back the work on our new school. An injury often sets a young player back for months. The pause set back a company trying to expand quickly.

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as others
verbs.wrong: To sell cars at a low price
verbs.why: New students work hard to catch up with the class. Small shops try to catch up with big online stores. Rivals such as Tesla and Amazon were trying to catch up with Waymo.

mainIdea.s: Waymo paused its freeway rides across the U.S. after California banned its driverless cars from state freeways. Officials acted because the cars kept entering areas where crews were working.
mainIdea.why: California stepped in after cars ended up in construction zones. Waymo then called off freeway rides everywhere and said the pause was temporary.

mainIdea.s: Driverless taxis hurt several road workers in a California crash, so the state stopped them on its highways. The company now says those trips will return once new software gets approved.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nobody was hurt. Waymo pointed out that no injuries or crashes happened in the construction zone.

mainIdea.s: Thousands of self-driving cars were recalled because a software problem let them go onto flooded roads. Engineers are now updating the system in each city where the company operates.
mainIdea.why: This is about a freeway pause. California stepped in after Waymo cars entered construction zones, and the company called off its freeway rides.

tf.s: Waymo called off its driverless rides on every U.S. freeway.

tf.s: Waymo said its freeway pause would be permanent.
tf.why: Waymo called the pause temporary and said it was working to bring back freeway rides.

tf.s: California officials stepped in because they saw a danger to the public.
tf.why: The state stepped in and called Waymo's freeway service an imminent hazard to public safety.

tf.s: People were hurt when Waymo cars ended up in a construction zone.
tf.why: Waymo pointed out that nobody was hurt and no cars crashed in the construction zone.

tf.s: Waymo said it wanted to look into how its cars were performing.
tf.why: The company stopped freeway trips outside California too so it could look into its cars' performance.

tf.s: Waymo's taxis also stopped driving on regular city streets.
tf.why: Waymo only called off its freeway rides. Its taxis continued to drive on city streets.

lines.text: Did you hear that Waymo {{called off}} all its rides on U.S. freeways?
California officials {{stepped in}} and banned them from every freeway in the state.
So the company decided to [[hit the brakes]] everywhere?
Pretty much. It says the pause is temporary. The ban {{kicked in}} on November 11.
But why did the state do it?
Three cars {{ended up}} in a construction zone near San Francisco, with nobody [[behind the wheel]].
No. Waymo {{pointed out}} that nobody was hurt and no cars crashed.
Still, I'd [[have second thoughts]] about riding in one.
There's also a video that seems to show one trying to {{get around}} highway patrol cars.
[[Call me old-fashioned]], but I want a person driving me on the freeway.
Waymo only {{rolled out}} freeway rides in 2025. Now it says it will {{look into}} how the cars are performing.
Does it plan to {{bring back}} those rides?
Yes, it's working with state officials. But this could {{set the company back}}.
Especially with Tesla and Amazon trying to {{catch up}}.
True. I guess these are the [[growing pains]] of a new kind of taxi.
